#7597. AI Labels Don’t Tell Consumers Whether An Ad’s Claims Are Real

Disclosure: Sourin Chakrabarti works on AI labeling for advertising at Meta. The views expressed are his own and do not represent Meta.

In October 2025, three clips appearing to show police detaining and pepper-spraying protesters racked up millions of views across X, Instagram and TikTok. Created with OpenAI’s Sora, the videos carried visible watermarks, yet NewsGuard found that users still cited them as evidence that the events occurred. The footage crossed an unsettling threshold: It didn’t just look realistic; it functioned as visual proof.

Most concern about deepfakes has focused on politics. But the same tactic is now appearing in advertising, where synthetic content can make a product claim look proven.

In a recent campaign investigated by Full Fact, a supposed doctor claiming to be affiliated with Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust tested a weight-loss patch and appeared to grow thinner on camera. The trust called the posts “completely fraudulent,” while Google’s Gemini detected SynthID watermarks confirming AI involvement. Yet that watermark only revealed that AI was involved, not where the fiction ended. Was only the doctor’s face synthetic? Or were the medical authority, hospital connection, personal experience and physical transformation invented, too?

This exposes the fundamental blind spot of AI disclosures: they flag the production tool, not the illusion. A generic label tells consumers that AI was used to build an ad, but leaves them to guess where reality ends and fiction begins.

The fraudulent NHS weight-loss ad was not an isolated incident. In 2025, the Australian Medical Association warned that deepfakes impersonating prominent doctors were promoting unproven products, with clinicians discovering the fraud only when patients asked whether to swap prescribed treatments for advertised miracle cures. In 2026, Chinese regulators launched an enforcement campaign targeting businesses that mass-produced fabricated consumer-experience posts.

The legal principle predates generative AI. In FTC v. Colgate-Palmolive Co., a shaving cream commercial used a plexiglass prop in place of real sandpaper. Viewers were misled because the simulation was presented as a genuine product test. The case offers a useful test for AI advertising today: Does an ad merely illustrate a claim or does it ask viewers to treat a synthetic scene as real-world proof?

Platforms and regulators are building substantial disclosure systems to track synthetic content. Google displays “How this ad was made” panels, Meta attaches “AI info” labels and TikTok offers “AIGC” self-disclosure controls. Governments are pushing in the same direction: The European Union’s Article 50 rules require transparency for synthetic media, China mandates explicit AI markers and New York requires advertisements to identify synthetic performers.

Yet current AI-labeling systems mostly tell consumers that AI was used, not what it changed or why it matters. The same label can appear on an ad with a decorative AI background and one with an entirely fabricated testimonial. Those uses are not equally misleading, but a generic label may not distinguish between them.

Some policies address the clearest cases. The Advertising Standards Council of India’s 2026 draft guidance identifies fabricated experts, endorsements and exaggerated results as high-risk uses that labeling alone cannot fix. TikTok Shop prohibits AI-generated professional identities used to sell health products and alterations that misrepresent product performance. But a harder question remains: What about AI simulations that are lawful but could still be mistaken for real-world evidence?

The disclosure gap is becoming urgent as AI ad generation reaches industrial scale. In 2025, advertisers created three times as many Gemini-generated assets on Google as in 2024, including nearly 70 million in the final quarter alone. Meta has reportedly aimed to automate ad creation and targeting with AI by the end of 2026. Because these tools are embedded directly into ad-creation systems, safeguards cannot rely on post hoc consumer complaints. They must operate systematically across millions of ads.

The answer is not to label every synthetic pixel. Building on the IAB’s January 2026 disclosure framework, regulators should adopt a risk-based approach requiring specific disclosures whenever AI material appears to provide evidence for a product claim. This approach would produce three outcomes:

Platforms could implement this approach by requiring advertisers to disclose three things: the role played by any AI-created person or scene, whether the generated material depicts product performance or results and what real-world evidence supports the claim. Meta, Google and TikTok already accept advertiser declarations, so these questions could fit into existing workflows. Platforms should also retain a record of the advertiser’s answers and the notice shown to consumers, creating an auditable trail of how each ad was reviewed and presented. An emerging industry proposal calls this a served disclosure receipt.

Consider the weight-loss patch video. Under this system, an “AI was used” label would be only the starting point. The advertiser would have to identify the doctor as a synthetic expert, classify the apparent transformation as a product-performance claim and clarify whether the testimonial represented a real customer. It would also have to provide evidence supporting the weight-loss claim. If the doctor was falsely presented as real, the testimonial was fabricated or the result lacked substantiation, the ad would not be approved.

The goal is labels that answer the question consumers actually face: not just whether AI made the ad but whether AI made up the reason to buy.

“Data-Driven Thinking” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.

#7595. Fox Doesn’t Want To Talk About Roku, But It’s Got Lots To Say About Tubi And Politics

Any investor hoping to ask about Fox’s pending Roku acquisition during its fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Monday was out of luck.

Fox’s IR rep made that clear up front and pointed analysts to Fox’s SEC filings instead.

However, CEO Lachlan Murdoch did share a mini update, including that shareholder and foreign regulatory approvals are in, although Fox is still working with the DOJ on antitrust clearance.

“[We] expect to close the transaction as soon as we can,” Murdoch told investors, noting that Fox’s “conviction in the opportunity has only grown.” Pairing Roku’s platform with Fox’s sports, news and entertainment content is a good recipe for building “our position in the fastest-growing segments of the media landscape,” he said.

Fox’s revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion in the quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue (60% in its TV segment) driven by the World Cup, early midterm spending and Tubi, its free ad-supported streaming service.

Tubi grew revenue 35% year over year, alongside a 23% uptick in total view time.

Fox attributed that engagement to a combo of Tubi’s content library, 10 new originals and a World Cup hub, which drew on Fox’s US English-language rights to the tournament.

Tubi also got a boost from viral content from more than 600 creators. Its Tubi for Creators program launched in 2025 with six creators and has since wooed big YouTube names like MrBeast and Jomboy Media.

And profits are growing, too, despite higher content costs, according to CFO Steve Tomsic, who noted that Tubi is contributing more to the bottom line than it was in the year-ago quarter when it turned its first profit – a development Murdoch himself apparently didn’t see coming.

A Bank of America analyst on the call reminded Murdoch that a year or so ago he’d said that Tubi’s growth, then in the midteens, wouldn’t be sustainable.

“I don’t remember saying that, but I’m sure I did … Thank you for calling me out on that one,” Murdoch said, adding that Tubi’s profit margins should settle in the 20% range once it reaches “further maturity.”

Advertising is the main engine behind Tubi’s momentum, which Murdoch said is continuing into the current quarter. Tubi’s audience is young, diverse and mostly cord-free, he said, which is like catnip for advertisers.

“They’re a very hard market for advertisers to reach,” he said, which, in a midterm year, is a pretty good pitch to political campaigns.

Fox booked more than $350 million in political ads this cycle, and Tubi was responsible for roughly $50 million of that.

Most of the rest – $250 million-plus – went to Fox’s local stations, including many in battleground states, where demand is so high that some stations run out of ad inventory. The remaining $50-ish million went to political ads across national sports, news and entertainment.

But if you squint, and not that hard, Tubi also kind of counts as local advertising in Murdoch’s view. “It’s effectively local revenue because it’s targeted,” he said.

Politics aside, sports has been a tailwind, too.

The FIFA World Cup final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history; the World Series, which aired on Fox, averaged 12 million viewers; and Fox’s NFL “America’s Game of the Week” is drawing an average of nearly 25 million viewers per game.

But Murdoch was also careful to temper expectations for Fox One, Fox’s streaming service for Fox content.

It’s not like there’s a World Cup every year – or a midterm election.

“It’s always a point in time,” Murdoch said. “Every couple years, you’ve got to be careful to understand the strength of the political cycle.”

And not everything at Fox was a win this past quarter, no matter how you spin it.

Fox News finished its fiscal Q1 as the most-watched cable news network, with 2.1 million primetime viewers and 1.3 million across all dayparts. But those figures were down 17% and 16% year over year, according to Nielsen, and Fox News was the only major cable news network to see declines. The slide has continued into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

Murdoch blamed tough comps against last year’s “tremendous news cycle,” which included the inauguration, Charlie Kirk’s assassination and DOGE-related drama. He compared this cycle to the 2006 midterms, when a second-term president was halfway through his term.

It’s not that viewers are defecting to CNN or MS Now, he said. They’re “just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall.” (Even so, Nielsen does show CNN and MS Now both up from last year.)

Meanwhile, cable advertising rose 8%, helped along by sports, but digital news ad revenue fell. Asked about that – we mourn you preemptively, open web – Murdoch pointed to Fox News Digital’s standing as the top news site in the US and called digital news a “hyper-competitive market.”

#7593. Instagram is offering YouTubers up to $500,000 to post with its new horizontal format

Instagram isn’t just chasing YouTube‘s TV watch time and ad revenue–it’s chasing its talent, too. The Meta-owned platform has offered to pay some YouTubers up to $500,000 to post videos with its newly announced long-form horizontal format “Features.”

According to Business Insider, Instagram has approached “select” YouTubers with a floor price of $50,000; others have gotten six-figure offers, and things top out at a half-million dollars.

“We’ve been public about the fact that we are funding Features content directly with some creators right now to support them,” a Meta spokesperson told BI. “The details of those deals are confidential, but we’re excited to see the content going live.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

It’s not clear how Instagram is paying out these amounts–per video, per month, or as one-time flat compensation. We’d bet the latter, and perhaps the pot’s sweetened with a promise to pay creators performance bonuses or an ad rev share if their Features content does well (especially on TVs, where pricier ads slots can pull in serious cash for platforms).

Meta already said, though, that it’s “too early to share a long-term monetization model [for Features], but we’re exploring ways for creators to earn from brands, fans, and Instagram, including performance-based incentives.”

Introducing Features earlier this week, Instagram hyped its established TV viewership, with VP of Product Tessa Lyons saying “people love to watch Reels together in their living rooms with their friends, so we’ve been working on a TV version of Reels.”

“[W]e know to do that well, we need more than just short-form video,” she added.

Insta chief Adam Mosseri chimed in Oct. 28 after concern from creators, tweeting that “[w]e understand the economics matter a ton, and are exploring multiple options to help long-form creators get paid.”

This YouTuber-bait program is perhaps one of those options.

People familiar with the deals told BI Instagram’s terms just ask creators to post their long-form videos as Features on the same day they upload to YouTube.

Reza Izad, who reps Kareem Rahma, Noah Beck, and more as co-founder and co-CEO of Underscore Talent, told BI these deals are an “exciting opportunity” for YouTubers. The money is part of that excitement, sure, but Izad said this is also an opportunity for creators’ content to get a boost.

“Every time there’s a new feature in these apps that the company’s promoting, people will have more opportunity to be seen because there’s going to be algorithmic preference to this kind of content,” he said. “And unlike short-form, there’s not a lot of abundance.”

What he’s saying is true: We already know Instagram plans to pump posts made with Clips as Reels (a tool that takes snippets of Features videos and posts them to Reels with a link back to the full long-form upload) on its Explore page, and in other areas around the platform.

Something to think about in all of this is that a major part of YouTube’s living room success is the relative attractiveness and easy UX of its TV app. Google has put stock into making the TV app a banger, and Instagram isn’t there yet.

As Mosseri put it, “We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app, which […] is going to take some time to get it right. But I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long-term.”

Creators looking for equal viewership across YouTube and Features will likely be disappointed–at least for now. But for the folks Instagram wants to pay, this is indeed a rare chance to get get cash for cross-posting.

#7589. Affle Acquires Perion For $420 Million, Because ‘Synergies’

If you ask the executive leadership of Affle and Perion why the two companies are merging, the answer you’ll get is “synergies.”

Tal Jacobson, Perion’s CEO, is well aware that the term has become a total cliche. “Every time I write an email and use ‘synergy,’ Google pops up and says people don’t like that word,” he joked on Monday, the day after Affle agreed to acquire Perion for $420 million in cash.

But even so, it’s the best shorthand for what each company is missing that the other can supply, he told AdExchanger.

Affle is an India-based holding company for mobile ad tech built around performance marketing, largely in emerging markets, while Perion focuses on CTV, digital out-of-home and retail media. Most of its clients are big brands and agencies in developed markets, mainly in North America.

For the past few years, Perion has been evangelizing the concept of outcome-based advertising with its clients. But there was a hole in its offering. “We never had good performance-driven technology for mobile,” Jacobson said. “Affle has pure technology just for that.”

For its part, Affle gets a foothold with the agencies, holding companies and brands that Perion already works with, said Sameer Sondhi, Affle’s CEO of North America and chief strategic investments officer.

Perion, which has roughly 500 employees, will operate as a wholly owned subsidiary under Affle and brings the combined company’s headcount to just over 1,000 people. Jacobson, who will stay on as CEO, said that everyone from Perion is staying aboard.

LUMA Partners advised Affle on the deal, which is expected to close in early 2027.

AdExchanger spoke with Jacobson and Sondhi about how the pieces fit, what happens now to Perion’s own string of recent acquisitions and why Jacobson would rather call this a merger than a sale.

AdExchanger: Why sell to Affle and why now?

TAL JACOBSON: We don’t think about selling. We think about merging – taking two successful companies and making them a bigger engine of growth. “Selling” has a negative connotation, like somebody gave up, and that’s not the case.

Neither of us has the growth potential separately that we have together. We’ve spent a few good months working side by side, and the teams are working very well together.

Why is $420 million the right price? Perion paid $100 million alone to acquire Hivestack in 2023, $65 million for Greenbids last year and $12 million for PRN, which does in-store retail media, just a few months ago.

TJ: It’s a tricky question. For a public company, the right price is what investors will pay, and I don’t believe Perion was valued correctly in recent years. So, if the public market doesn’t see our long-term potential, why not join forces with someone who does?

The price doesn’t reflect the full long-term value; it reflects a point in time, and Affle wouldn’t buy this if it didn’t think the potential was bigger than the price.

SS: Both of us are listed, so the number is always going to be debated. There are plenty of public reference points – DoubleVerify, Nielsen, LiveRamp, IAS – and the boards have to approve. In the end, a number is a mindset thing.

Affle has been pushing a cost-per-converted-user (CPCU) model, where advertisers only pay for conversions. Will Perion’s DOOH, CTV and retail media inventory be sold that way?

TJ: Not necessarily. It depends on the channel and the customer’s goal. You can’t sell out-of-home on a CPC model, because you can’t click on an ad. But you can say, “Pay us for performance.”

Some formats might be CPC, others CPA or CPL. Whatever helps an advertiser’s business, that’s what we want to focus on.

So not CPCU, exactly, but a CPCU mindset?

TJ: We’re outcome-driven. The KPI is whatever defines success for that advertiser.

SS: With the targeting you can do on DOOH screens and the signals we get from mobile, the goal is to help clients with whatever way they’re used to buying. We don’t want to confuse them. We want to educate them.

Perion’s open web spend fell by around 23% in Q2. Doesn’t seem like a good sign for the future of the open web.

TJ: We’ve been telling investors and clients that the open web is not the future. Forget channels; focus on outcomes. When a CFO approves a budget, they don’t care if it’s websites or out-of-home.

And yes, everybody’s hyped about CTV, but if it doesn’t help the business, it doesn’t matter.

How much of this deal is about agentic AI?

TJ: Both companies have invested a lot in AI over the past two years. Our Outmax agent trades media, mostly in walled gardens, and Affle’s AI is focused on the deeper funnel and conversions. I don’t think we’ll merge the algorithms into one, but it helps to have all those tools under one roof.

SS: The systems don’t need to unify; they just need to talk to each other better.

Perion has made several acquisitions of its own and now it’s being acquired itself. How do all the nesting dolls fit together?

TJ: Affle lets every company it acquires stay independent under its own name and with its own road map and team. We’re not combining everything. Greenbids, for example, gives us the walled gardens – YouTube, Meta, TikTok – which neither Perion nor Affle had. PRN is just another extension of out-of-home, but inside retail stores.

The point is to sit in front of a CMO and be able to say, “Whatever you need, we probably have it.” We’ve worked hard over the past three years to roll up other companies, and this is just another phase of that.

This industry does not need 150 ad tech companies. It needs to consolidate.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.

#7586. OpenAI May Not Be So Open For Long; Prediction Markets Bet On Endorsements

OpenAI has been following the classic walled garden platform playbook for its ChatGPT advertising business. But people often forget that the first few pages are about opening up ad inventory to third-party intermediaries – before the walls go back up, of course.

YouTube allowed third-party ad serving … for a time. Facebook bought and then quickly shuttered the Atlas ad server. Amazon Prime once had a DSP partner program with full third-party programmatic visibility – but then dataxu, one of its partners, was acquired by Roku (so, buh-bye). The Trade Desk, the only other vendor in that program, was quietly cut off a few months later.

OpenAI may now be at that same early point in the cycle. The Information reports that Magnite and PubMatic have signed deals to “fill unused ad space” for ChatGPT. And they’re just the latest additions to OpenAI’s growing roster of ad-tech partners, which already includes LiveRamp, Criteo, StackAdapt and even Amazon Ads.

But this partner push has a pointed subplot: OpenAI’s VP of partnerships, Samantha Jacobson, was until recently The Trade Desk’s chief strategy officer. Jacobson announced her departure in May amid TTD’s painful exodus of senior executives. Now she’s helping build partnerships at one of the most coveted new media platforms in the world.

At TTD, the reaction may very well have been: “Don’t be a stranger. Seriously.”

Prediction markets Kalshi, Polymarket and Novig want to be household names. So they’re trading on the reputations of their celebrity spokespeople.

The sheer number of celebrities signing on to promote these controversial companies proves that the concept of “selling out” is officially dead, writes Amanda Mull at Bloomberg.

Consider a star-studded ad campaign Polymarket launched in September, featuring sports megastars Lebron James, Derek Jeter and Eli Manning, actors John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario, director Spike Lee and supermodel Emily Ratajkowski, to name a few. Or Novig’s headline-grabbing campaign with actress Sydney Sweeney.

It makes sense for Polymarket and Novig to associate themselves with these names, Mull writes. A March poll by Ipsos found that just 20% of respondents were familiar with the platforms, despite extensive marketing.

But what makes less sense is why celebrities would promote these companies, Mull argues. The same Ipsos poll found that, among consumers familiar with prediction markets, 40% viewed them as bad for society, while 60% thought they were no different than gambling.

Celebrities used to avoid tying themselves to such brands. But in this era of intensely devoted fandoms, “celebrities and influencers announce new ad campaigns and brand sponsorships to excited, congratulatory fans as though they are awards,” Mull writes.

So, if every celebrity is selling out, there’s nothing to criticize, she adds. “Maybe that’s why so many people agreed to be in that Polymarket ad at the same time – safety in numbers.”

Ad buyers are scrutinizing their Google search budgets more than ever, Digiday reports. And for good reason, too. Now that AI Overviews are encouraging users to click through at lower rates, those ads aren’t performing as well as they once did despite higher CPC rates.

One marketing expert told Digiday that he’s seen some advertisers reallocating 10% to 30% of their Google search budget into other channels. Others claim that some of their clients have started moving money into Meta and ChatGPT or into other Google products, including AI Max, YouTube and Demand Gen.

That shift in advertiser spending seems to mirror similar trends happening at Google overall. Last week, Alphabet’s stock price dropped over 10% after the company’s latest earnings report revealed a slowdown in search advertising revenue growth, which SVP and Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler attributed to lower monetization of its AI Mode.

Meanwhile, Google is sticking to its assertion that AI-powered advertising campaigns and a more “conversational” search experience will ultimately provide greater value to advertisers in the long run. Which assumes the company won’t run out of money by then – a pretty fair assumption, given that it earned $127.6 billion in Q3 this year alone.

#7584. This Ad Tech Company Wants To Ensure Brands Don’t Go Viral For The Wrong Reasons

Some marketers say that “all press is good press,” but odds are, they wouldn’t be thrilled if their brand was the next to go viral for a blatantly offensive ad.

Ad tech company Digital Culture Group’s goal is to stop those ads before they ever go live by preemptively determining what sort of creative and messaging will resonate with – or offend – an audience.

Its flagship product, the Audience Resonance Index (ARI), uses a range of first- and third-party data to determine what kinds of people will be most interested in a product, and how to connect with them through current cultural trends.

In late September, Digital Culture Group launched a new module within ARI called Resonance Studio. The new module takes the product a step further and predicts how creative will perform – including specific critiques customers may have and how to fix them – before it goes live.

Alongside Resonance Studio, Digital Culture Group also launched the ARI 100 Ad Pledge, which offered 100 pro bono creative assessments to brands and agencies.

The launch of the module and the associated pledge came on the heels of the Converse controversy in September in which the sneaker brand received backlash for an ad featuring imagery that many viewers said clearly evoked the KKK and lynching.

Converse pulled the ad after two weeks, but the damage was done, with some longtime Converse fans throwing away – or even burning – their shoes and posting to social media.

It was “an extremely unfortunate thing for the Converse team to experience,” said Crystal Foote, CEO and founder of Digital Culture Group, but it was also horrible for “the communities that were impacted by that.”

Foote uploaded the ad to both ChatGPT and to ARI, asking each one to rate the ad and provide feedback. ChatGPT gave the ad a B minus and said that it “would not classify this creative as culturally insensitive or recommend suppressing it on cultural grounds alone.” Rather, its only critique was that the depiction of the sneakers “could be interpreted as gender non-conforming styling” (the horror) which could offend some viewers.

ARI, on the other hand, gave the ad an F, citing “hate symbols” including robes and hoods that could evoke KKK imagery. It also noted that “the dangling shoes could be read as echo of hanging or lynching imagery” and could offend Black Americans and descendants of lynching victims, said Foote, quoting the model outputs directly.

In terms of how to fix it, ARI suggested what seemed obvious to many: Avoid white robes, cone-shaped hoods and dangling feet. Instead, position the product in a shoebox or on a shelf.

ARI is trained on data from sources ranging from the American Community Survey (an annual demographic survey) to eMarketer’s predictive analytics to research from Nielsen’s cultural team, said Foote. The model is trained to recognize historically offensive or non-resonant imagery before a current customer ever lays eyes on it.

It also has a social listening feature, so it can tap into conversations happening on social platforms including Reddit, X and Meta.

Since the Converse ad was already live, and ARI was likely influenced by real people’s reactions to it. But ARI and Resonance Studio would ideally be able to predict – and prevent – an outcome like the one Converse faced even before the ad went public, due to its ability to denote the offensive imagery.

The predictive analysis was a big draw for humanitarian organization Care.org, which began working with Digital Culture Group in September and participated in the ARI 100 Ad Pledge.

Care submitted two pieces of creative to ARI for analysis: one in support of its National Women’s Day campaign, and one encouraging people to contribute financially to the company’s care packages.

For the National Women’s Day campaign, Care submitted an ad it had used in the past which emphasized the importance of providing opportunities for women globally and in various professions. Its focus was “leveling the playing field” for all women, “from the sports field to the farm field to the conference room,” said Mary Kate Wilson, Care.org’s associate VP for creative and content marketing.

The ad’s call to action asked viewers to sign a pledge that would “level the playing field for women and girls everywhere,” said Wilson – but ARI determined that Care’s audience needed more.

The ad needed to be more specific about where, exactly, the signatures were going, like whether they would be added to a petition or sent to a legislator. People want to know, “What difference do I make by lending my signature to this?” Wilson said.

The second ad focused on the history of the care package, which was created toward the end of World War II by an American cooperative (which later became Care.org) that sent food packages to families in Europe.

ARI gave the ad a high score on cultural relevance and receptivity, since it emphasized multiculturalism and different types of care packages, depending on a community’s needs. But where it had room for improvement was making it “more time-bound to today,” Wilson said.

Again, people wanted to know where their dollars were going, what the resulting care package would look like and who it would serve.

Sensitive industries – particularly those that cater to people’s health – require more than just accurate targeting, said Joy Allen-Altimare, president of women’s health and sexual wellness brand Vella Bioscience.

For Vella (another brand participating in ARI’s pledge), “cultural understanding” is a key marketing focus, including who is represented in the ads and challenging outdated stereotypes and stigma around discussing topics like menopause.

One of the ads it submitted for review was for its Meltwater product, a vaginal moisturizer made with hyaluronic acid and aloe vera.

The ad was “really trying to be an ingredient story” and emphasize the ways that moisturization and restoration can apply to intimate areas, said Allen-Altimare. In many ways, Resonance Studio determined that the ad was effective. The predicted click-through-rate was 106% of Vella’s benchmark goal, and the psychographic alignment (or, how well the ad would resonate with its intended audience) was estimated to be around 85%.

However, Resonance Studio determined that there was room for improvement around model inclusivity, regarding age and race. Since the messaging was focused on ingredients, only one shot in the ad included a model. ARI suggested incorporating multiple images, or a video where several women interacted with each other, to diversify the ad and connect with a wider range of women.

When developing a “product storytelling moment,” Vella wants to ensure it’s representing consumers of various ages, sizes and races, said Allen-Altimare. Plus, she said, there’s an added barrier of having to use ambiguous wording around pleasure and intimacy, since most ad platforms are strict about the way they can portray sexual wellness products – particularly ones that target women.

ARI’s Resonance Studio “will help us understand if we’re talking to ourselves,” Allen-Altimare said, or if the ad is truly making sense and resonating with the women it’s trying to reach.

If you ask the executive leadership of Affle and Perion why the two companies are merging, the answer you’ll get is “synergies.”

A combo of Tubi, sports and political ads powered Fox’s growth this last quarter, even as Fox News lost viewers and the Roku deal awaits DOJ clearance.

It’s fall, and M&A is in the air. Two acquisitions happened this week: Stagwell bought Freestar, and DoorDash bought Instacart.

Starting in Q4, Reddit will test logged-in-only mode to protect its user engagement, improve ad targeting and keep AI from scraping its content.

DoorDash on Thursday confirmed the rumors and announced its intention to acquire Instacart at a $17 billion valuation.

#7568. Ignition, Inc.: MSP Mac Help Desk Guru (work from home)

Ignition is one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and the only fractional IT firm that specializes in the venture-backed technology ecosystem.

Fully Remote · Work from home · Full-time (Eastern or Pacific time zones) · Apple-first

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

⠀ You'll be the front line: helping with what you can, researching what you can't, and pinging the rest of the team when you're genuinely stuck. That last part is a skill, not a weakness — knowing when to ask is half the job.

We're one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and one of the only certified Apple Premier Partners — that’s kinda like getting knighted by the ghost of Steve Jobs. We started where you’d expect to find Macs (creative agencies, non-profits, education) but our primary clients today are cutting-edge, venture-backed AI SaaS startups, VC and private equity firms, registered investment advisors — many of them operating under stringent compliance expectations (SOC 2, SEC). That means we hold ourselves to a higher standard than the scrappy shop we started as. Polished, reliable, security-minded work is the baseline now — but always with a smile!

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We teach each other what we know, cover for each other when life throws a punch, and care a little too much about doing things the right way. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

We move fast, priorities shift, it’s not always documented (whatever it is), our tool set and list of supported platforms is sprawling, and some days the to-do list is longer than you'd like. If you can stay warm under pressure, create order out of chaos, learn new stuff fast because you love it, and speak up when you need help, you'll thrive here.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. As they say, the price of freedom is eternal vigilance.

The tech you'll work with (and grow into)

Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

Yes, PCs too — about one-third of our users are driving Windows

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 admin consoles

Identity and access — SSO, MFA, and security keys (Okta, Entra ID, Yubikey, and friends)

Lots of other security tools — our stack is constantly evolving and may vary from client to client

The everyday productivity stack — Slack, Zoom, conference-room AV, networking basics (Meraki), and endpoint tooling

⠀ You don't need to know all of this. You need to be the kind of person who wants to. As you grow, there's a clear path into infrastructure administration, project architecture and implementation, and — for the right person — security and compliance work (phishing simulations, endpoint detection, SOC 2 / CIS / SEC readiness, due diligence questionnaire support, etc.). That's where our most senior people live, and it's wide open.

The hard requirements — we won't move forward unless you:

Can work standard business hours in Eastern or Pacific time zones (we currently need both)

Have a quiet home workspace and reliable broadband

Have proven Apple aptitude — you actually use and like the Apple ecosystem

Have at least 5 years of IT support experience on the job.

⠀ Everything else — and this is the longer list, on purpose. We figure technical skills are teachable; character takes a lot longer. So we're looking for someone who:

Genuinely cares — about clients, teammates, and doing right by people

Loves to learn, and proves it in how they spend their time

Reads, and writes clearly — clear writing is clear thinking, and you'll do a lot of it

Stays calm and kind with a frustrated person on the other end of the line

Can tell the difference between good customer service and fantastic customer service, and refuses to settle for the former

Notices when something's being done inefficiently and fixes it (you may boast about it later, that’s fine)

Proofreads their own work (yes, we noticed whether you proofread your application)

Has a sense of humor, and doesn't take themselves too seriously

Our company founder/CEO is headquartered in the Bay Area. We work with innovative, ambitious companies developing AI products. Our team members hold a range of opinions about whether AI is “good or bad” for humans, but at the end of the day, we embrace the plain fact that it is here, we must embrace it to evolve, and our clients increasingly depend on us to help them embrace it, too, to help them evolve and stay competitive.

Our CEO's opinion: AI will not replace human labor any time soon; rather, AI is a new opportunity to either (a) get things done faster, or (b) get a much higher quality of output than before. If you’re an AI tinkerer, great! We want to hear how you’re using it and see your latest vibe project. If you’re allergic to AI or have no interest in learning new habits to work effectively with it, this is not the place for you.

Base salary: Applicants outside the USA will be compensated according to your local employment market. For applicants closer to the junior side who are located in the USA, $50,000–$65,000/yr, depending on experience level and your local geographical price index. With experience, comp goes up from there. Genuinely experienced, more senior candidates can be slotted higher — let's talk.

Type & location: Full-time, work from home, fully remote. Eastern or Pacific time zones.

Benefits: Medical / dental / vision for the employee, 401(k) with employer contribution, 2 weeks of PTO annually to start, and a stipend for your home internet.

The first step is really easy and only takes 10 minutes — no resume, no cover letter, no essays. Here's how:

Take this online Culture Index assessment (about 10 minutes): We use it to screen for people whose natural wiring fits how our team works.

If your profile lines up with what we're looking for, we'll reach out and ask you to complete a 60-minute TestGorilla assessment for critical thinking skills, send us your resume, and maybe a couple of other items.

From there, we conduct between 2-4 video interviews. One of these might be a live technical assessment.

If the Culture Index step feels like a strange way to start a job application — that's kind of the point. Remember the phrase Think Different?

Ignition is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome and will consider all qualified applicants. Good luck in your search — and may the Force be with you!

No forms. Just smart, optimized applications.

#7565. Shopify Now Lets Stores Pay The Company Behind Your AI Shopping Agent via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Explore Ahrefs’ Q2, Q3 2026 AI search benchmarks and practical next steps.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Shopify pays the company behind an AI agent 0.3% of promoted-product orders, and stores can add more. Here is what that commission changes.

If I send an agent to buy something for me from the Shopify catalog, is it finding the best possible product for me, or the product that will make whoever is behind the agent the most money? As of Oct. 27, 2026, Shopify’s documentation gives the agent a reason to work for two others besides me: the company that built it, and Shop, Shopify’s app and website.

Shopify mixes products that pay a commission into the search results its catalog gives AI agents. It calls them promoted placements. When a shopper buys one, Shopify pays the company behind the agent (Shopify calls it the developer) 0.3% of the order.

Stores can pay more. If a store runs Shop Campaigns, Shopify’s paid promotion program, and turns on external platforms, Shopify turns the store’s campaign “into a commission” on top of the 0.3%. In search results, the total comes back with the product, next to its price, rating, and review count. Shopify’s example shows 1.5% on one product.

Shopify pays the store’s extra commission “only when the buyer completes the purchase in Shop, either in the Shop mobile app or on shop.com.” For those products, the links the agent gets point to shop.com, not to the store’s website. A sale on the store’s website earns only the 0.3%.

So the agent has a reason to pick the product that pays its developer more, and a reason to send me to Shop to buy it. Shopify’s documentation doesn’t say whether a bigger commission also moves a product up the list.

In my test, two Claude models went with the numbers they were given: at their default settings they picked a water bottle listed with 447,221 reviews 84 times out of 100, when the store’s product page showed 6,537. I haven’t tested a commission number. What an agent does with one depends on its model and on what its developer tells it.

Shopify asks developers to label promoted products, to say they may earn a commission, and to make that clear “before buyers act on a promoted result.” It points to US FTC rules on paid relationships and to EU and UK rules on ads and sponsored content, and leaves the exact wording to the developer.

The FTC, EU, and U.K. rules were written for ads and paid recommendations. The FTC’s endorsement guides say a paid connection behind a recommendation has to be disclosed when people wouldn’t expect it. The closest EU rule I found bans search results that hide “payment specifically for achieving higher ranking” (Directive 2019/2161). An agent picking one product isn’t clearly a recommendation in the FTC’s sense or a search result in the EU’s, and a commission on a sale isn’t clearly payment for a higher ranking. I’m not a lawyer, and I know of no ruling either way.

Shopify calls promoted placements a Developer Preview, which developers join from a waitlist, by invitation. The extra commission applies only to products in an active U.S. campaign, in USD. Shopify’s documentation doesn’t name any developer that has joined. Developers outside the program get ordinary results, so I can’t see promoted products from the outside either. Shopify says the details “are not final and might change”.

What I’d watch is whether Shopify says a bigger commission moves a product up the list, and whether any agent tells the shopper what it earns and where it is sending them to buy.

This post was originally published on No Hacks.

#7564. A new California law lets children of family vloggers make their parents take down all footage of them

A new California law will protect the children of family vloggers once they turn 18.

Senate Bill No. 1247 gives adults whose parents, legal guardians, or family members used them in social media content while they were minors the right to demand removal of said content.

Once served a notice of removal, parents/guardians/etc have 10 days to take down violative content or edit it to remove the requester’s appearances. If those 10 days pass and the content is still up, vloggers will face penalties of $3,000 per day moving forward, plus further potential damages, injunctive relief, and attorney’s fees.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Now, to be clear, this law won’t let someone take their mom to court for posting Facebook pictures of them in an embarrassing Halloween costume (though we do think parents should more carefully consider what they post about their kid online, especially in the age of AI).

S.B. 1247 has a couple requirements that tune it to specifically target professional family vloggers.

We’re guessing it could potentially apply if a parent signed a financial agreement with a family vlogger to have their kid appear in the family’s content on a regular basis, but that circumstance isn’t accounted for in S.B. 1247’s current form.

The law will also lay a mandate on social media platforms: Once it kicks in, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and all other sites “shall provide a clear and conspicuous mechanism by which a child influencer can request a vlogger” remove content featuring them, according to the bill’s text. If a platform doesn’t have a built-in mechanism, it has to be responsible for receiving removal requests, and is required to forward those requests to vloggers within three days of receipt.

Vloggers who receive removal requests and comply with them will not face any consequences. It’s only if they refuse removal or if removal takes longer than 10 days that they open themselves up to further legal action.

This law kicks in in January 2027–and while it’s only a California law, we do expect other states might enact similar protections. YouTube just turned 20 years old, so the vlogging industry has now been around long enough that thousands of kids whose parents once featured them in videos are turning 18 and gaining control over their own lives. S.B. 1247 makes sure that control is retroactive, too.

#7562. 7-Eleven made a micro-K-drama to promote its new noms

7-Eleven is going full microdrama to promote its latest munchies lineup.

Starting Nov. 2, 60-second episodes of A Convenient Love will pop up on 7-Eleven’s TikTok and Instagram channels to promote its new “Flavors of Korea” menu.

The mini K-drama follows two classmates whose destinies intertwine during late-night runs to (of course) the local 7-Eleven. A short trailer captures a 7-Eleven employee/classic Korean uncle telling the two not-so-star-crossed lovers that they should notice: opposites attract.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

He delivers this line holding what is arguably the centerpiece of 7-Eleven’s new collection: a KBBQ pizza that’s an official partnership with Korean frozen food brand bibigo.

“K-dramas run on heightened moments. And some of the most memorable ones happen over something as simple as a late-night meal at a convenience store,” Danny Lee, A Convenient Love‘s director, said in a statement. “That’s what made 7-Eleven’s new Korean-inspired menu a natural fit. We built 7 vertical episodes around it and shot all of them in a real 7-Eleven with the food at every turning point. In this genre the style is core to the storytelling, so we leaned into those familiar devices with some American cinematic flair, from the characters and humor to the visual details and, of course, the food from 7-Eleven.”

Pizza aside, the Flavors of Korea collection includes a gochujang remix on 7-Eleven’s iconic egg salad sando, gochujang boneless wings, bibigo spicy chicken dumplings, a KBBQ taquito, a KBBQ hot dog, and somyeon with kimchi.

7-Eleven will drop Convenient Love episodes throughout November, and each installment will “feature a limited-time discount on a spotlighted menu item,” according to a press release.

We have of course seen other brands capitalizing on the microseries trend, but 7-Eleven might be hitting the sweet spot. Microdramas got off the ground in Asia, and K-dramas specifically (long- or short-form) are an international sensation. Combining the two could push A Convenient Love to a level other branded series have yet to reach. We’re curious to see how it pays off.

Yo, 7-Eleven: Hit us up with performance data when the series wraps. (We also wouldn’t mind a sando or two.)

#7560. Discord Member Messages May Start Showing Up In Google In December via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Explore Ahrefs’ Q2, Q3 2026 AI search benchmarks and practical next steps.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Discord's most public servers will each have a web page that may carry AI summaries and some messages search engines can show.

Discord announced that every one of its most public communities will have a web page starting Nov. 16, and those pages may show AI-written summaries of their public conversations. From mid-December, some members’ messages may also show up on those pages and in Google and other search engines.

The announcement covers what Discord calls Discoverable Servers, which it says number more than 63,000. They’re public communities that anyone can join without an invite. To qualify, a server needs at least 1,000 members, has to be at least eight weeks old and must meet Discord’s activity and safety requirements. Summaries and messages are both on by default, and admins choose which public channels take part.

Admins have until Nov. 16 to change these new channel settings before summaries can begin showing up.

Members are allowed to opt out of having their posts display on public pages (in some regions, this is the default).

On Nov. 16, all Discoverable Servers will have a Server Web Page. Discoverable Servers have already had the ability to create an optional server web page; others which don’t currently do so will be assigned a default page based upon their current server profile. Discord’s help page says anyone can view one, and search engines like Google can show it.

Those pages may also carry Channel Summaries, which Discord’s admin help page says it creates using AI from recent discussions in public channels. The same page says the summaries “may not always be accurate.” They cover conversations from Nov. 16 onward and don’t show usernames.

From mid-December, Discord says some messages from public channels may appear on server pages and in web search, in members’ own words and without usernames or avatars. The rollout is gradual, and it may be a few weeks before the first messages appear. Messages sent before mid-December aren’t included.

Messages in threads and forum posts are included when the parent channel is public and participating. Private threads and private forums are never included, regardless of the parent channel’s settings. For now, messages appear as text only.

Server settings include switches and lists for administrators to manage Channel Messages and Channel Summaries under Community > Web Presence. Each of these items has their own unique switch and channel listing. However, private channels (including those restricted to certain roles) will always be omitted.

Admins may disable the community’s discoverability; this action will revert the community back to a normal Community Server. As long as a server is discoverable, its Server Web Page will remain available. In order to eliminate access to this page, an administrator will need to turn off the discoverability option.

Additionally, turning off this feature will only affect new messages posted after such actions take place. Previous messages can still be viewable until they are deleted. Upon deletion of a message, the message will no longer be accessible within the application nor on the Server Web Page; however, Discord says it cannot guarantee that search engines will not retain cached or indexed versions of the deleted message.

Discord’s robots.txt file shows the sitemaps for its server pages and its announcement pages where posts from pilots have appeared. The pilot testing of Channel Messages has been running on several gaming servers (including NBA 2K, Rust & Dead by Daylight) with admins and moderators as writers of every single message posted.

Dead by Daylight’s server page, accessed October 29th, contains ProfilePage structured data. This is the same profile markup Google rolled out in November 2023, in addition to the discussion forum markup I reported about at the time. Admins are encouraged to “accurately and specifically” describe their servers, per the Server Web Pages help page, so searchers can find them.

As of Oct. 29, there are no rules in robots.txt referencing AI crawlers; however the general restrictions do not cover the paths to the server and announcement pages.

Discord’s FAQ answer on whether it sells messages to AI companies reads:

No. Nothing has changed. We are making Discord content easier to find if admins and users choose to make their content available on the web.

As of Oct. 29, all three help pages listed above, as well as the announcement referenced above, do not reference AI crawlers or model training.

Any Discoverable Server you run will have a public page starting Nov. 16, whether or not you create one yourself. The channels you leave enabled in Web Presence determine which conversations Discord’s AI summarizes there, so it’s a good idea to review them before that date.

Discord’s own examples of answers that can show up in web search are game builds, strategies and boss guides. In August, I reported that Ahrefs’ data put public Facebook Groups second to Reddit among sites in Google’s Discussions and forums results. Some server pages can already show up in search, but the member answers Discord describes don’t start rolling out until mid-December.

Default server pages and summaries can go live on Nov. 16, with Channel Messages beginning to roll out in mid-December. Once member messages are available, you can check whether those pages include discussion forum markup, just as server pages include profile markup.

#7558. Fox News attacks the media roughly every 15 minutes, our study finds. (CNN? Every 140 minutes.)

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.”

In 2025, trust in journalism reached a record low. According to Gallup, only 8% of Republicans expressed trust in the news media, compared with 51% of Democrats. New data show an uptick among Republicans, but overall trust remains near this record low, and the gap between Republicans and Democrats remains substantial.

One of the key drivers of this lopsided decline in trust in journalism may be the extent to which news outlets spend time bashing other news outlets, or bashing the news media in general — a phenomenon we call inter-journalism disparagement. Our research team at Duke University’s DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy recently completed a study of the prominence of this phenomenon on each of the “big three” cable news networks (CNN, Fox News, MSNBC/MS NOW); whether it has increased or decreased over time; and whether there are significant differences in the rate of disparagement across networks.

The results were stark. Fox News far exceeds the other networks, with inter-journalism disparagement taking place once every 14.5 minutes. In contrast, CNN engages in inter-journalism disparagement roughly every 140 minutes, and MSNBC every 61 minutes.

To conduct this analysis, we gathered 15 years of cable news transcripts (2011-2025) for each network. We gathered a random sample of one week’s worth of programming for each year.1 With this approach, we ended up with 3,543 transcripts and almost 19 million words across the three networks, which equates to roughly 62,000 pages of text.

Given the volume of text to be analyzed, we trained OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 to identify attacks against the news media. We developed a 20-page instruction document to help the model code instances of disparagement. GPT-5.5 consistently achieved 99.5% accuracy at identifying inter-journalism disparagement and 100% accuracy for avoiding false negatives, compared to human-coded samples. (You can read more details about the entire training and analytical process here.)

We defined inter-journalism disparagement as negative statements about the conduct or content of an explicitly identified journalism target (such as a specific news organization, or the news media in general). Our definition, which is described in greater depth in the full paper, needed to be quite detailed in order for ChatGPT to produce accurate results. Examples of inter-journalism disparagement include:

What we found when comparing the three networks tells us a lot about the dynamics of contemporary cable news and partisan journalism.

First, Figure 1 shows the rate of journalism disparagement across each of the big three networks. Because the volume of text that we analyzed varies across each network, our primary metric was the rate of disparagement per 1,000 words of transcript text. In this figure, we show not only the rate per 1,000 words, but we also convert that rate into a time-based frequency, using the industry standard of 1,000 words equaling approximately six minutes of air time.

In Figure 2, we graph the frequency of inter-journalism disparagement over time. Here, we see that the massive difference between Fox News and CNN/MSNBC persists over the 15-year time period. Still, we do see some dips in the volume of disparagement on Fox News in the two-year periods leading up to the 2016 and 2024 elections, with journalism disparagement levels on Fox News rebounding to near-peak levels in 2025. We haven’t figured out yet what to make of this pattern.

CNN and MSNBC seem to converge in their disparagement activity starting around 2017, with MSNBC’s disparagement rate decreasing somewhat, and CNN’s disparagement rate increasing somewhat. This pattern aligns with recent research that has shown, in other contexts, that CNN and MSNBC programming are converging in ways that suggest diminished differences between the more “centrist” CNN and the more left-leaning MSNBC.

A key takeaway here is that we should not think about Fox News and MSNBC as flip sides of the same partisan journalism coin. At least in relation to inter-journalism disparagement, these left- and right-leaning cable networks behave very differently. Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.

In order to get a deeper understanding of these differences, we also identified the targets of the disparagement. These results are presented in Figures 3 through 5.

Figure 3 presents a breakdown of the most common targets of disparagement on Fox News. By far the most frequent target of disparagement on Fox News is “the media.” Following in a distant second is CNN, with the “mainstream media” rounding out the top three targets. Other relatively frequent targets include The New York Times, MSNBC, and The Washington Post.

As should be clear, Fox News devotes far more attention to disparaging journalism as an institution than it does to attacking individual news sources. This stands in stark contrast to what we see when we look at the results for CNN and MSNBC. Looking first at CNN, Figure 4 shows that the network’s most frequent target is Fox News (though with a frequency that wouldn’t crack the top three of the Fox News list).

Similarly, as Figure 5 shows, Fox News is also the number one target on MSNBC. Both CNN and MSNBC have the same top three, with Fox News followed by “the media” and the “right-wing media.” These instances of institutional disparagement happen far less frequently on CNN or MSNBC than they do on Fox News.

Finally, we were also able to identify which hosts or anchors were the most frequent disparagers of their fellow journalists. Those results can be seen in Figure 6. Given the lopsided amount of inter-journalism disparagement on Fox News, it is not surprising that this graph is dominated by Fox News personalities, with Sean Hannity taking the top spot, followed by Greg Gutfeld and Tucker Carlson (note: our graph for Howard Kurtz reflects his move from CNN to Fox in 2013).

This study didn’t distinguish further in terms of the nature of the disparagement across the three networks (for example, in terms of severity or legitimacy). This is something we are exploring in the next stage of this work. Nor did we examine whether viewer exposure to inter-journalism disparagement reduces trust in specific outlets or the institution of journalism. That certainly seems like a reasonable assumption, given the dramatically lower levels of trust in journalism among Republicans that we noted at the outset. We plan to investigate this relationship directly in future research.

But what we do see in this research is that disparagement of the institution of journalism, and of particular news outlets, is a much more prominent component of Fox News programming than it is of either CNN or MSNBC. Some researchers have proposed that this kind of high-volume disparagement of news sources that don’t tow the same partisan line takes us beyond traditional notions of partisan journalism and into the realm of “anti-media media.” The goal of anti-media media is to “weaponize the facade of journalism against the roles assigned to journalism” in a democracy. Based on our findings, Fox News fits this characterization.

Philip M. Napoli is the James R. Shepley Professor of Public Policy, director of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy, and director of undergraduate studies for the journalism and media minor in the Sanford School of Public Policy at Duke University. Adam Meskouri is a politics researcher at Harvard and Duke. Anjini Mani is an undergraduate at Duke. Grant Socol is a graduate research assistant at Duke. Harrison Walley is an undergraduate at Duke. Rather than analyze the entirety of the networks’ output over this time, we created a “constructed week” for each year, which is a common practice in this kind of content analysis. This involves selecting a random Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, etc. within each year, so that the sample of programming was reasonably representative of the year as a whole. We included all programming across all dayparts in our constructed weeks. Note: MSNBC was only available through 2023; the network became MS NOW in late 2025. [↩]

#7557. So you’re a creator, and you want to know: When is the magic moment to sign with a manager? We have your answer, straight from Viral Nation’s Head of Creator Relations.

Imagine this: You’re a small-town mom with two kids, working long shifts while your husband goes back to school. Time is short and money is tight, so your household is constantly on the hunt for new meal-prep kitchen gadgets.

Then you find one that makes your life infinitely easier–but when you look online, no one is talking about it. So, you record a quick video and post it to your Instagram or your TikTok. You think it’ll be a nice recommendation for your friends.

Instead, the video blows up. You get 50,000 followers overnight and a message from TikTok about monetizing your content. The brand that made the gadget pops into your email, asking if you want to collab.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

This sort of scenario has played out for thousands of people. It’s not always a product review, and it’s not always one overnight hit, but thousands of creators have found audiences online that turned out to be bigger than they expected.

With the creator economy generating more than $250 billion annually, it’s only natural for these folks to start thinking about turning their content into careers.

A talent manager is one of the key people who can help make that happen–and onboarding with a manager is often a major inflection point for a creator.

There’s no one-answer-fits-all, says Chloe Morris, Head of Creator Relations at Viral Nation Talent. Morris has more than a decade of experience in our space, and at Viral Nation, she helps identify promising creators who’d be great additions to their roster.

“I was on a panel at VidSummit, and the follow-up question from a lot of creators was, ‘At how many followers should I be before seeking representation?'” she says. “I’d say it’s one of those things where metrics aren’t the only thing that comes into play. It’s really the creator identifying when they need support, and that level of support can vary. It can differ depending on the creator, their goals, what they’re looking to achieve long-term, and also identifying their own skill set, and what they enjoy.”

She adds a perhaps surprising piece of advice: “I encourage a lot of creators to have at least one [solo] brand deal under their belts before seeking representation.”

The point of this is giving creators the opportunity to “know what they enjoyed about the process, and where they feel they need help.” Doing at least one brand deal on their own “is going to help them identify when they need representation and who that representation is,” she says.

Once that brand deal is done, Morris generally considers the creator to be in the second stage of their journey. The first, she explains, is meeting the thresholds necessary to start earning revenue from platforms (think YouTube’s AdSense or Twitch’s affiliate status).

This second stage is “where an agency really comes into play,” she says, because “you’re moving to the next level of monetization, which is working with brands. You’re doing things like integrations, sponsorships, becoming a brand ambassador.”

Agents can be critical in managing increased brand communiques and making sure contracts are in everyone’s favor.

This second stage of monetization sets creators up for the third stage: “releasing something around your own IP, whether it’s a book or a tangible product or a podcast,” she says. “Brand deals’ value is being able to show that you can push product and you have an influential relationship with your audience.”

All this being said, Morris notes that creators should always be in control of how much management they want to receive.

Sometimes they’re comfortable with their following as it is, and email handling and contract negotiations are all they need. Sometimes they want more intense production help, like booking filming venues, hiring staff, or upgrading to better equipment. Sometimes they want to expand to brand deals outside their niche, or look at putting their content on FAST channels.

And sometimes creators want full-fledged career coaches who can help them strategize every step while they grow their viewership and build a personal brand.

Viral Nation offers all these levels of support–but though Morris of course wants creators to come on board there, she says they should always feel comfortable investigating their options.

“I always joke that shopping around for an agency is a bit like speed dating,” she says. “You get on a lot of different calls, you ask the same questions, sometimes you get different answers. Ultimately, your agency should be an extension of you and your brand, and you want to make sure it’s a good alignment.”

If the alignment is good, a manager will fill one very crucial role: #1 cheerleader.

“The reason an agency is working with a creator should be because they’re a fan of the creator and the art that creator is putting out,” Morris says. “Find representation that really empowers you to keep doing what you do best.”
