AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Measure whether AI recommends your brand to buyers, fix outdated sources, and connect your place on its shortlists to signups and pipeline.

Tony Uphoff ran a test this month that every SEO and brand manager should copy before next year’s planning starts. He asked ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews the questions his prospective clients ask, then counted how often the answer engines recommended the two businesses he launched in February.

The results were humbling. Across 59 answers, his newsletter, Uphoff on Media, showed up in zero of 12 category answers. His firm, Uphoff Advisory, showed up in one of 43. Yet every engine that answered “Who is Tony Uphoff?” knew his career.

Tony said “The models know who I am. They almost never recommend what I’ve built.” That gap, between being known and being recommended, is the measurement problem I think most of our industry is still getting wrong. Tony’s test shows you how to find it in your own brand, and three other posts he published in October explain why your CFO, your next acquirer, and your next employer are about to care about it.

A disclosure first. Tony and I worked together at Ziff-Davis from 1988 to 1993, and he’s since been CEO of five businesses. He was brought in to transform Business.com and ThomasNet.com, led the carve-out of Pipeline360, where he now serves as a board advisor, and today writes Uphoff on Media while running Uphoff Advisory.

His audience is B2B media, marketing, and technology operators, not SEO specialists. But read his last four posts back to back, and you’ll find a five-time CEO working through the same questions this column keeps asking about AI search, from the other side of the table.

Bill Ziff taught a generation of us at Ziff-Davis to separate events from trends. Tony’s October 7 headline, “AI Stopped Being a Story. Now It’s in Your Multiple,” is that lesson in 10 words. When AI shows up in the valuation of a company, it has stopped being an event.

See also: The Click Economy Is Over: How AI Search Is Forcing Publishers To Rethink Revenue

Tony’s argument starts with a sequence change in B2B buying. “The machine drafts the shortlist. The human validates it.”

The survey data backs him up. In G2’s March 2026 survey of 1,076 B2B software buyers, 51% said they now start their research with an AI chatbot more often than with Google, up from 29% in G2’s 2025 report. 69% said a chatbot led them to choose a different vendor than they had planned, and one in three bought from a vendor they had never heard of before.

Here is where Tony makes the point I’d underline for every SEO reading this.

“For two decades the scoreboard was discoverability. SEO taught every marketing team to rank, earn the click and get found. Most companies carried that scoreboard straight into AI.”

They ask a model about themselves by name, get an accurate answer, and conclude they’re covered. Tony calls that a false positive, and his own results prove it. A well-known founder or a legacy brand makes the business feel visible. Ask what a buyer would actually ask, and the company rarely makes the list.

In my columns on YouGov’s AI brand research, I’ve kept coming back to one idea. Awareness is not the metric that tells you who is winning. Consideration is. Tony’s discoverable-versus-recommended split is the same funnel distinction, measured inside the answer engine.

If brand recognition is doing that little of the work, then a report built on branded queries is measuring the wrong thing.

See also: Brand Protection In AI Search: How To Audit And Defend Your Brand’s Identity

The second finding should worry anyone who has been through a rebrand, a merger, or a leadership change. Tony called out that “all three engines that described me still call me CEO of Pipeline360.” Only one mentioned the firm he runs now. He explained, “The sources included org-chart aggregators, executive databases and old press releases.”

Tony’s rule of thumb is blunt. Answer engines default to what the web has said about you most often, “and most often usually means longest ago.”

That stale record costs twice, because the machine uses it to decide whether to recommend you and the human uses it to verify the machine. Few teams are watching. A Corporate Ink study reported by eMarketer in May found only 29% of marketers actively track and measure AI visibility.

There’s a second lesson buried in Tony’s test. When he asked the engines “What is Demand-as-a-Service?” all three defined it accurately and cited Pipeline360’s own pages. None mentioned Tony, who helped create the strategy. He’s fine with that, because the company owns the category language. But his conclusion is the one content strategists should tape to the monitor. “The models credit whoever publishes the clearest explanation, not whoever had the idea first.”

See also: AI Visibility Measurement: What To Track & What To Ignore

The one time Uphoff Advisory made a list, ChatGPT ranked it second of four for “Who advises founders of B2B information and data businesses?” The broad questions returned nothing.

The citations explain why. On category questions, the models rarely cited the firms they named. They cited roundups, the “best AI newsletters” and “best B2B marketing podcasts” lists published by Zapier, Content Allies, and others.

Tony points to a May 2026 study by Maryanna Franco and João da Silva on Friction AI’s platform that found the same mechanism at scale across 14,140 queries about activewear brands. Nike and New Balance share the same Google Knowledge Graph description, yet Nike appeared in about 71% of athleisure recommendation answers and New Balance almost never did.

This is where I’d push back on Tony a little. Nineteen prompts run for one week is a snapshot, and AI answers shift from run to run. One appearance in 43 could be a floor or it could be noise, and a single week can’t tell you which. His plan to rerun the same prompts in January and publish the numbers either way is exactly right. I’d go further and track it weekly, because Citation Share of Voice only means something as a trend line.

Tony’s October 7 post introduces the Q3 2026 Uphoff Value Index, his quarterly benchmark of what buyers pay for B2B information, marketing, and technology businesses. This quarter he added a score for AI Disruption Protection built on four questions. The third one stopped me.

“Relationship ownership. Do you own the customer relationship, or rent it from search and platforms?”

Tony cites Collingwood’s 2026-27 Market Report, a survey of about 100 active acquirers, in which 91% called the AI resilience of a business model essential or important and 74% said the same of a direct relationship with the customer. In his worked example, two data businesses with identical P&Ls are valued at 5.6 times EBITDA ($28 million) and 4.0 times ($20 million). The only difference is whether buyers believe AI can route around them.

I read that third question as the most direct challenge to how many of us have pitched organic search for 20 years. To an acquirer, traffic that arrives from Google and leaves without a login, a subscription, or a first-party record is a rented relationship. In my view, the SEO teams that thrive in this cycle will be the ones that can show how search converts rented visits into owned relationships, not the ones with the biggest session counts.

Tony’s October 19 post, “Before You Flatten the Org Chart, Make Sure You Can Measure What AI Delivers,” uses Block as its case study. By his math from Block’s reported figures, the company produced $10.36 billion of gross profit with 10,205 people in 2025, about $1 million per person. Its raised 2026 guidance of $12.51 billion with just under 6,000 people works out to about $2.1 million per person.

The benchmarks he cites matter more for most Search Engine Journal readers. The average marketing agency does about $163,000 of revenue per employee. The median public software company does about $395,000. In Tony’s index, two agencies with identical P&Ls, one with 68 people and one with 40, are now about $1 million apart in value.

Tony describes a spectrum from honest signal to performative signal. Contract value, expansion revenue, and churn sit near money. Form fills and self-reported data sit at the cheap-to-fake end. Then this.

“A lead score isn’t a fact about someone’s business. It’s a fact about how well your content ranks.”

That’s an uncomfortable read for anyone whose monthly report leads with rankings and organic sessions. If you want to move from SEO manager to director, my advice is to rebuild your report, so it starts at the honest end of Tony’s spectrum and works backward to the search metrics that explain it.

Tony’s Oct. 14 post, “Your AI Pilot Doesn’t Have a Job,” borrows a phrase from Darshan Deshmukh of ProcureAbility on the Art of Procurement podcast, “death by a thousand pilots.” The diagnosis is that teams lead with the technology instead of the outcome. Tony cites BCG’s 2024 finding that roughly 70% of the challenges in getting value from AI come from people and process, 20% from technology, and only 10% from algorithms.

SEO teams are buying AI visibility trackers right now, often on a corporate card, which is precisely the pattern Tony warns about. His Application Test has three gates, cleared before any money moves. State the job in plain words with no vendor name in it. Name the owner and the baseline. Set the one signal you’ll check in 90 days, and decide in advance whether you’ll scale, fix, or stop.

“Track our AI mentions” fails the first gate. “Get us onto the AI shortlist when buyers ask for our narrowest category phrase” passes it, and Tony’s own 1-in-43 is what a baseline looks like.

Tony closes with a five-move sequence. Here’s how I’d adapt it for SEO teams:

Add a recommendation rate to your scorecard, and report it first. Write 10 to 15 prompts the way your buyers ask them, built around the category, the problem, and “who should I hire for.” Add two or three branded prompts. Run them across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and AI Overviews, and track how often you make the list and whether the description is accurate. Run it weekly, not once, so you’re reading a trend rather than a snapshot.

Fix the record the models read before you chase the shortlist. Pull the sources the engines cite when they describe your brand. Update the pages you control, including bios, LinkedIn, and the press page, and request corrections from the aggregators and directories you don’t. After any rebrand or leadership change, assume the models haven’t heard.

Own the narrow phrase, then earn a place on the lists. Pick the most specific way a buyer describes your problem and publish the canonical explanation under your brand. Then find the 10 to 20 roundup and comparison pages the engines cite in your category and give someone a target for getting on them. That’s a digital PR job, and it’s the job SEO and PR should have been sharing all along.

Tony and I haven’t worked at the same company or attended the same meeting for 33 years. But, from a certain point of view, we never stopped working on the same problem, which is getting the right name in front of the buyer before the buyer goes looking.

What’s changed is who builds the shortlist. My bet is that the teams still reporting rankings first will spend 2027 explaining a pipeline gap that their dashboards never showed them. The models are drafting your buyer’s list right now. Make sure you’re measuring whether you’re on it.

#7554. “We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours”: USA Today Co. execs defend Palantir deal

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

USA Today Co. executives are revealing new details about a controversial deal with Palantir. In a joint interview with Fast Company’s Alex Pasternack, three executives from the country’s largest newspaper chain explained why they moved ahead with the Palantir deal despite major opposition from their own employees.

RELATED ARTICLE“An inherent conflict of interest”: More than 800 USA Today Co. employees want the company to end its new Palantir partnershipHanaa' TameezAugust 10, 2026Mike Reed, the chairman and CEO of USA Today Co., previously said that the deal — first reported by Nieman Lab’s Hanaa’ Tameez — is part of a larger shift the company is making to become “an intelligence organization.” At a Palantir conference last month, Reed said that the company’s services were a way for USA Today Co. capitalize on “the shift to online and the data we have on consumers,” Pasternack reported.

In this new interview, USA Today Media president Kristin Roberts detailed some of those services for the first time:

In all of our entertainment stories and our sports stories, we do affiliate links to our partners. So if you’re reading a sports story, you want to buy the jersey for that team, our reporters and editors used to have to go to a file, find a relevant link, copy that link, put it in. All of that is now automated, and that’s a Palantir project.

Lark-Marie Anton, then a communications executive at USA Today Co., chimed in, saying that Palantir’s current scope of work is focused on audience and advertising, but in the future that could extend to social media strategy and reporting tools.

What stood out about Palantir was its ability to create what it calls an ‘ontology’ layer — essentially a unified model that allows different datasets and systems to work together and be acted upon in real time….The challenge isn’t collecting more data, but making better use of the data we already have.

In August, more than 800 USA Today Co. employees from 31 unionized newsrooms called on the company to dissolve its partnership with Palantir. In a statement, staffers named ethical issues and uncertainty over how the software would be used. Throughout the Fast Company interview, Reed and Roberts heavily criticized the NewsGuild and internal efforts to oppose the deal.

Roberts leveled the strongest criticisms of USA Today Co.’s unions across the country, going as far as to say the NewsGuild was lying to its members:

Guild leadership is saying things that are factually untrue. They prey on fear. No matter that I will appear in front of any newsroom for a standup in which they ask me anything for an hour and a half at a time, and I explain to them all of the things.

I’ll give you an example that’s incredibly real for us. Palantir doesn’t work inside of any USA Today Company system. They don’t have access to any of the notes our reporters take. They’re not in the Microsoft suite of tools. They don’t have information directly about our consumers or our staff….They don’t work in our systems. We feed them highly controlled data. We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours.

Reed doubled down on these accusations, extending them to the work the NewsGuild has done organizing around AI in the company, including its push for clauses that would protect journalists from layoffs due to AI adoption.

“I think we’re having more success in newsrooms that are not unionized, with this new world, than those that are unionized,” Reed said.

Last month, USA Today Co. made significant layoffs across the company, including at its local newspapers, and reorganized its audience team. Reed, in a memo to staff, referenced AI-related traffic declines as a reason for the layoffs.

“USA Today Co. executives’ animosity toward their workers and unions is nothing new,” said NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss in a statement to Fast Company. “[We] fully stand behind the statement workers released when this deal with Palantir was first announced.”

You can read the full interview on Fast Company.

RELATED ARTICLEIn Medill’s latest State of Local News report, a “festering, 20-year-old problem” looms larger than everSophie CulpepperOctober 22, 2025If you thought last year was bleak, Medill’s annual State of Local News Report is here to ring the alarm bell louder.

What was a “creeping erosion” has now “mushroomed into a full-blown super El Niño-like event for local news, leaving widespread and long-lasting displacement in its wake,” writes Tim Franklin, founding director of the Medill Local News Initiative, in his introduction to this year’s report, released Tuesday. The Northwestern University team’s research “paints a portrait of a local news ecosystem in a state of precarity.”

In the past year, Medill tracked 26 new news deserts, “the largest single-year rise by far since Medill began keeping records five years ago,” Franklin writes. The previous year, only six new news deserts emerged.

Medill’s team says to understand that acceleration, you have to look at where newspapers are disappearing fastest now. While about 70% of the papers that disappeared over the past 20 years were based in urban or suburban communities, in recent years a greater share of newspaper closures have happened in smaller, rural and poorer communities, according to the report.

“When the news disappears in these counties, it stays gone,” the report states.

RELATED ARTICLELast year, Illinois started giving local news outlets tax credits to support journalism jobs. A new report looks at how it’s goingSophie CulpepperFebruary 9, 2026Many of the new news deserts emerged because of small rural papers shuttering in the Midwest. In fact, the report notes that Illinois lost more newspapers than any other state: 30 newspapers shuttered in the state between July 2025 and August 2026, “all small to medium-size outlets.” That means nearly one in five of the 170 newspapers that shuttered in that year was based in Illinois. The state’s losses are especially notable because it enacted one of the first public policies to preserve and grow local journalism jobs in 2024.

“Independent owners of small to midsize newspapers especially were already operating on a knife’s edge,” Brier Dudley writes in his examination of newspaper losses in Illinois. “This past year, their slim margins were squeezed by shrinking revenues and steeply escalating prices for newsprint, fuel and other materials.”

The price of newsprint rose nearly 18% over the past year, Dudley reported, as U.S. mills closed or stopped production of newsprint. That’s about five times the national rate of inflation, he noted. As of April, the United States has just one newsprint producer left.

A few other highlights from this year’s report:

The extreme urban-rural divide: “Virtually all the new news sources are in urban areas, while rural America is increasingly arid news and information territory,” Franklin writes. “And virtually all the philanthropic support for local news is in metro regions.” The report notes that there are fewer than 50 counties in the U.S. “that lack a newspaper but feature an alternative digital or broadcast outlet.” Of the 287 news outlets to start up in the last five years, nearly 80% are in urban areas.

Traffic declines: Digital readership is in “precipitous decline” for many outlets. According to Comscore data from more than 700 local news sites, monthly traffic has dropped by an average of nearly 2 million pageviews, or almost 30%. Meanwhile, traffic to 100 of the largest local newspapers has declined by almost 50% since 2022.

Local TV news: This year, for the first time, Medill’s report included local TV newsrooms. The team identified 678 local commercial TV newsrooms across the country. The overwhelming majority are located in metro areas with existing local news outlets. (“Adding commercial television to the LNI database made little impact on which counties we identify as news deserts,” the team notes.) TV news is already highly consolidated — the five largest owners control more than half of newsrooms, and the 10 largest control 75% — and further consolidation is underway, if Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna survives an antitrust lawsuit. The deal would merge the second- and fourth-largest owners of local commercial TV newsrooms.

#7551. Reddit CEO Ties Search Referral Drop To Google AI Mode via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Explore Ahrefs’ Q2, Q3 2026 AI search benchmarks and practical next steps.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Reddit says search referrals are falling and its CEO points to Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode. Here's what its login test means.

Reddit told shareholders Thursday that its search traffic dropped by more than 1 million referrals per week, on average, during October. That followed a third quarter in which search referral traffic was “down meaningfully.”

On the earnings call, CEO Steve Huffman said the biggest part of Reddit’s working hypothesis is Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode. Reddit also plans to start testing a logged-in-only version of the site in select markets outside the U.S. this quarter.

Huffman said the test is partly meant to decide how much of Reddit people can see before a login prompt, including people who arrive from search. Where Reddit draws that line will decide what a logged-out searcher sees after clicking a Reddit thread from Google in the test markets.

Reddit’s third-quarter letter says the search referral decline sped up late in the quarter and continued into October. Logged-out and web traffic took the biggest hit, with some carrying over to logged-in and app traffic because search is a common way users come back to Reddit.

The letter puts October this way, using DAUq for daily active uniques:

“During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week. If this rate of decline continues, current trends would suggest that total DAUqs could fall in Q4, by a low-double-digit percentage from our current base of 130 million DAUqs.”

The letter doesn’t give the weekly referral count that decline is measured against, and it doesn’t break the decline out by search engine.

Reddit’s daily active uniques held at 130.3 million globally from the second quarter to the third. In the U.S., they fell from 53.2 million to 50.7 million.

The U.S. decline was in logged-out DAUq, which fell from 30.1 million to 27.3 million between the second and third quarters. Logged-in U.S. DAUq rose slightly, from 23.1 million to 23.4 million.

Outside the U.S., DAUq grew 24% year over year. Chief Operating Officer Jen Wong said Reddit raised international marketing spend partly to make up for reach lost from search referrals.

Three months earlier, Reddit’s second-quarter letter described search referrals as “choppy,” with traffic more volatile late in that quarter.

Asked what was driving the Google traffic changes, Huffman said Reddit’s hypothesis has two parts. The biggest is AI Overviews and AI Mode, which he said Google appears to be expanding aggressively in the U.S. and elsewhere. At a minimum, he said, they push other results down the page.

The second factor is machine-translated content, which he said Reddit believes is being ranked lower, mainly affecting traffic outside the U.S. He added that this doesn’t look like the kind of algorithm change that comes and goes, though Reddit doesn’t have visibility into that. Neither the letter nor the call says how much of the decline Reddit attributes to each factor.

Reddit’s CEO said demand for Reddit hasn’t changed. The word Reddit is still among the most-searched words on Google, he said, and “Google is crawling us as hard as ever.” He also said AI Mode “does not drive traffic,” not for Reddit and, as far as he knows, not for anyone else.

I reported in July 2024 that a robots.txt change left Google as the only major search engine able to show Reddit’s newest posts. Reddit had signed a data licensing deal with Google earlier that year.

Asked about data licensing with Google and OpenAI, Huffman said Reddit is in active discussions with no update to share, and that not doing a deal is one possible outcome.

Reddit’s letter says it will begin fully testing a logged-in-only experience in select markets outside the U.S. in the fourth quarter. Neither the letter nor the call names the test markets.

The letter says logging in will help users find more relevant content and give Reddit more signals for ad targeting. It also says the change protects access to Reddit’s corpus of data and helps the company adapt to emerging regulations. On the call, Huffman said the vast majority of scraping happens through logged-out access.

He said Reddit needs to find the right boundary “to provide value to the user, whether they’re coming from a shared link or maybe from search themselves or trying out Reddit.” He said some version of Reddit will be available before a hard login prompt, and that Reddit wants shared links to keep working.

“This is a test, but we are going to make this transition,” Huffman said. He said Reddit will likely trade reach for engagement.

Logged-in and app users account for over 80% of Reddit’s monetization, according to the letter. Third-quarter revenue grew 53% year over year to $895 million.

Reddit also plans to keep converting search-referred mobile web users to its app. Only about 13% of eligible mobile web users currently see the app conversion prompt, according to the letter.

Asked whether brands advertise on Reddit to show up in AI models, Wong said Reddit is “pretty skeptical of GEO,” or generative engine optimization, and fairly resistant to manipulation. GEO isn’t part of Reddit’s advertiser partnerships today, she said.

See also: Google Reveals How AI Search Is Reshaping What Users Query

Reddit’s figures on lost search referrals are a first-party look at clicks from search on a site whose threads rank across a wide range of Google queries. Huffman described Google’s AI features as the biggest part of Reddit’s hypothesis for the decline.

A Reddit thread that ranks in Google has generally been readable without an account. In the markets where Reddit tests logins, that will depend on where Reddit puts the login prompt.

When Reddit’s login tests start in select markets outside the U.S., the first thing to watch is how much of a thread a visitor arriving from Google can read before a login prompt. Reddit says the results will inform “an optimized version of logged-in-only Reddit globally.”

Reddit will also keep reporting logged-in and logged-out daily uniques by geography, CFO Drew Vollero said Thursday. Its fourth-quarter 2025 letter had said Reddit planned to phase that reporting out this year.

Follow on YouTube. Matt G. Southern is the Senior News Writer at Search Engine Journal, where he’s covered Google, SEO, ...

#7550. When Slate went back to its 1996 homepage, it learned some web design lessons for 2026

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate, now 20 years old, reflects on the value of taking the long view and not chasing digital media trendsShan WangSeptember 23, 2016The fonts are Times New Roman and Arial Narrow, the colors are maroon and mustard, and the cursor is the 8-bit pixel hand. When Slate revived its original 1996 homepage to celebrate its 30th birthday this fall1, the team found a lot to like besides nostalgia.

“I’ve read Slate since 1997, when I finally had access to my own computer at my first job,” Hillary Frey, Slate’s editor-in-chief, told me recently. At the age of 51, she said, “I’m speaking as an old. But I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

Slate’s homepage has long functioned as a “fossil of what the internet was during that time,” said Ivylise Simones, Slate’s creative director. In 1996, Slate was trying to figure out what a magazine on the internet should even look like; in 2026, it’s among the last general-interest digital-native news sites, and print magazines are dying out. “Salon is one of our only lasting contemporaries,” Frey noted. “There are other sort of fellows from that era, like Feed and Nerve. They’ve been gone for awhile.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate launches a metered paywall to draw more membership revenue from readers, not just listenersSarah ScireMarch 26, 2020In its 30th anniversary campaign, Slate has found its fossil-like nature to be something of a selling point. (It can also be a challenge.) Over the years, the site has published a number of posts about its history and editorial and design choices. A decade ago, then–news editor Chad Lorenz wrote “A history of Slate in nine home pages.” (At launch, Slate articles included page numbers and printing instructions.) A 1998 paywall, Lorenz wrote, was “fortunately” abandoned by 1999. But the paywall returned in 2020. (It was metered at the start, but today it’s dynamic, changing based on user behavior.) For its 30th birthday, the site is running a promotion: a year of access for $19.96.

RELATED ARTICLECan’t read just one: Slate’s daily advice columns are strange, funny, deep, and increasingly a major traffic driver for the siteLaura Hazard OwenJuly 22, 2019“Going back to our roots, there are certain elements we are starting to really love,” Simones said, and she’s thinking about how to include them in the site’s ongoing redesign. She likes the spareness and simplicity of earlier versions of the site, she said, pointing to Reddit and Discord as places that are “more reminiscent of old homepages than the current, very stylized, very gridded layout” found across the internet. A less dense homepage on desktop, she said, is “refreshing.”

“Our editorial guiding light is the mix,” Frey added. Slate has verticals, but they’re not emphasized in the story selection at the top of the homepage; instead, life, politics, and advice stories are mixed together and weighted similarly. “Having an image for every story you share on the homepage is just not necessary,” Simones noted.

Some 1990s-era headline styles still work, too, Frey has found. One of her favorites is a 2002 piece by Slate founding editor Michael Kinsley: “The secret vice of power women.”

“He was writing it about his wife, who found tremendous satisfaction and relaxation in watching police procedurals,” Frey said. “That’s something I still identify with, though most of them now are from Finland and Norway. 100%, this headline would play on the Slate homepage right this second.”

Art courtesy of Slate A wrinkle for 2026: The 1996-inspired homepage had to work on mobile, even though nobody was reading Slate on a phone 30 years ago. [↩]

#7548. Two creators went to NYU’s business school, then decided to make a show about the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“Our videos are what we wish we could consume more of.”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

On a September afternoon in Manhattan’s Union Square neighborhood, Shreyas Sinha is sitting on a toilet, wearing a blue suit. Looking into the camera, he asks, “Why is it that everything I’ve been eating this year is giving me diarrhea?”

Sinha is about to link the 2026 cyclospora outbreaks to decades of problems at the Food and Drug Administration. “I’m only allowed to make three diarrhea jokes in this video,” Sinha says. “I live in tyranny.”

The toilet video is one of the tamer stunts that Sinha and his co-creator, Gaurav Srivatchan, have pulled for their YouTube channel, A Show About The News, a weekly deep dive into major business and politics stories (tagline: “Critics are calling it the worst alternative to mainstream media, and those are just the critics I’m related to.”)

In a video about why young people can’t afford to buy homes, Sinha pops out of a cardboard box on the street and takes former New York City mayor Eric Adams to a studio apartment filled with men. Other recent videos include a 45-minute interview on the street with former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci, an explainer on prediction market ads, and a rap music video on why retirement investments are safer than get-rich-quick schemes.

Sinha, 25, and Srivatchan, 22, met in 2023 when they were students at New York University’s Stern School of Business. They teamed up to make short vertical explainer videos, but those didn’t take off as much as they’d hoped. In 2024, Sinha quit his finance job to pursue A Show About The News full-time, and they transitioned to creating long-form deep dives with a dash of their own humor.

I chatted with Sinha and Srivatchan about how they launched their media careers, how they use humor to explain the news, and what they think business opportunities are for creators today. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Tameez: Why did you start creating news videos? Sinha: Gaurav and I started making videos together during the spring 2023 semester, when I was a senior at NYU and he was a freshman. I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. It seemed like everything was [pointing to], “Hey, you should start making short-form videos.” And then Gaurav was like, “Hey, I’m actually really good at editing videos.” We were not really thinking of it as a YouTube channel, but as making short-form stories. At the time, we were called Fifty50 Media. We were all about trying to distill the world into bipartisan perspectives. We eventually started focusing more on deeper-dive stories. We renamed ourselves to A Show About the News. It’s very easy to put out a political opinion that goes viral, but we really wanted to focus on good stories. Eventually, we started making videos for Morning Brew, and we joined Morning Brew full-time as a franchise in August 2025.

I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. Srivatchan: We realized that building a loyal audience off shorts wasn’t feasible in the long-term. And we constantly [faced] the challenge of bringing in nuance. That’s one of the reasons we started working on long-form videos. We try to bring in the political economy lens from our college education and highlight the underlying principles [of] today’s headlines. Sinha: To be honest, we weren’t successful in short-form. We had made 50 or 60 shorts… Srivatchan: Some of them would pop off, get a million views. But the way people consume on the internet is very different from the way people consume when they go to a theater, [where] they’re paying for an experience and they’re going to watch a specific thing. YouTube and social media are like a theater where you can leave and go watch another movie at any time. That’s the challenge of making videos on the internet.

Sinha: After our first video that got a million views, we were like, “Oh shit, this is it.” And it wasn’t. We added followers, but it wasn’t like we were going to get 100,000 people to come back in the next short. We were competing against the new Frozen movie and The Office and Mr. Beast exploding dynamite in his backyard. Tameez: Tell me more about how the Morning Brew deal happened. Srivatchan: I was in London, studying abroad. I slapped a bunch of logos as watermarks on our old videos [and sent them as] demo reels to news outlets. Sinha: We literally got zero responses…then an opportunity came to make a video for [Morning Brew] and it was a great experience. We made another and another, and then they were like, “You guys should just do this for us.” Srivatchan: Morning Brew provided us access to this office. It’s great to not meet under a lofted bed in Shreyas’ apartment. Sinha: They’re an excellent partner [because] they believe in allowing editorial control to be with the person who makes the video. We’re not going into meetings asking, can we do this topic next week? It’s a very high-trust environment, which, from talking to other people who work at other media companies, is extremely rare. Tameez: You guys both left careers in finance to do this full-time. Sinha: It was an economically stupid decision, but I knew that if I failed now, I would be young enough to start again. It’s easy to have the golden handcuffs of waiting until the right time, but there is never a right time. It was taking a bet on myself and someone who I really trusted. Still, our videos were getting 12 views at that time; it wasn’t as if something took off and it was like, “Okay, this can pay our bills.”

Srivatchan: I had the advantage of being younger. [Shreyas left] a full-time job. I did my summer internship in consulting and got my return offer, but it was a lot less of a risk for me, personally. It obviously helped that we had some backing from Morning Brew. Tameez: Why is making A Show About the News important now? How does it fit into the larger information ecosystem? Sinha: What we do, in the context of where we went to school, is the equivalent of becoming ballerinas. All of my friends are investment bankers in private equity or in consulting. That is the tried and true method [for NYU Stern graduates]. If you tell people, “Hey, I’m not recruiting for banking, I’m thinking of doing consulting,” they look at you like you just said you want to be an art major. When we said we were going to build a media company, it was truly mind-boggling for people. I loved what Fareed Zakaria did, what Ezra Klein did, but my favorite people when I was a kid were Jon Stewart and John Oliver, Hasan Minhaj and Seth Meyers and Conan O’Brien and Nathan Fielder. I knew I wasn’t going to be a great stand-up comedian, I wasn’t going to be a great writer, but maybe I could combine those to make a job out of it. It’s easy to pat ourselves on the back and say there’s a lot of garbage out there. But also, it has never been a better time to be an independent creator. If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there.

Srivatchan: When it comes to shorts, either Shreyas or I will have something that really interests us for the week. We start scripting it, then we switch the scripts and each of us does a pass on the other’s. Then we revise them and film them. That takes roughly two out of five workdays. We spend the rest of the time on long-form. We’re also doing a weekly livestream to discuss the headlines with the audience and build that audience connection. So our output is two native short-form, one long-form, and one live stream per week.

Sinha: Do we actually have something new to say about it? There’s no point in making a video that someone else has already made.

A lot of people have made videos about how people aren’t having kids anymore. That doesn’t mean we wouldn’t [cover that topic], but we need to have something new to say. In our video, we talked about how governments have spent tens of billions of dollars but it hasn’t resulted in any more babies. We talked about demographic trends and got into studies. We brought in a bunch of 19- and 20-year-olds and asked them why they’re not having more sex. Then we went to a bunch of older people and were like, “So, you guys were doing it hella in the 90s. What’s the secret? Let’s give it to these kids.”

Sinha: We try to be funny, maybe to a deficit. In one of our worst-performing videos, we had a guy come in on an inflatable horse. Gaurav was wearing a Will Smith mask and slapped me. But sometimes it really works. We filmed this thing where we were having a shootout with Abraham Lincoln as he smoked a vape. That did great for us.

I listen to a lot of podcasts of serious, smart people. The way they talk, I’m like, how are you not ripping your hair off right now? How are you not just slamming your head against your desk?

Srivatchan: We have all these sources that we regularly read. For a lot of politics and inside scoops on Capitol Hill, Politico is great. For more niche stories, ProPublica is great. Each source has its own strength. We send stuff to each other all the time.

Once we’re in the research phase of a video, we do everything possible to learn about what the scope of the video is and what sources and articles can fall into that.

Sinha: We do a lot of our own fact-checking. Corrections often occur in the way of Gaurav coming to me and being like, “Shreyas, you moron, you said this and it’s actually this.” Then we record a voiceover, or we change it in the captions, or we just put it up as text.

Sinha: If you go on YouTube right now, high production quality is the expectation. It’s not like when I was young and my favorite YouTubers were clearly filming in their bedrooms. There’s so much money that is being invested into it, which is awesome, but if you want to have authentic relationships with your audiences, you need to do more.

Srivatchan: Earlier this year, TBPN [Technology Business Programming Network] was sold to OpenAI for $100 million. Their whole thing was live-streaming. They didn’t get that many viewers concurrently on their livestreams — everything was clips, targeting a very specific niche — but we saw how they grew through clips.

Sinha: When we started making these videos, I was writing articles on the side and freelancing so that I could pay rent. Eventually, this was able to pay rent.

By no means are we rich. But we really believe in the business model of digital media. It’s important to incentivize people to invest in media that is fact-checked, that is telling stories that are new and not just polarizing or viral for virality’s sake. You can’t ask people to only think of [media] as a charity expenditure or as a nonprofit, because those are the first things that go away when the market goes down, and the first thing people are going to stop cutting checks to if they don’t see the ROI.

We spend most of our time thinking about content, but it’s important to be creative about our business models. We always tell ourselves not to think about ourselves as employees or YouTubers, but to keep reminding ourselves that we’re founders of a startup that is trying to do something for the world.

The prevailing narrative that news media is doing poorly is because news media for generations was run by journalists, and that was fine because they could get cable carrier fees. But the reason they were able to do that was because they had a monopoly. You could only watch CNN, CBS, and ABC News because that’s all you had.

[I asked Sinha and Srivatchan to answer a few final questions via email. Their answers are below.]

Sinha: It’s hard to say what’s legacy and what’s new these days. Morning Brew has never had a TV broadcast or print media arm, but it’s owned by a media conglomerate, Axel Springer. Other news companies, from CNN to The Wall Street Journal, have pretty successful social media presences and journalists who’ve made a name for themselves.

The crisis for news companies that dominated in the 20th century is that they relied on fixed distribution: cable, broadband, local stations, and papers. A random Joe couldn’t get their ideas placed in those, so the competition for viewership was highly limited.

Today, competition is high. Legacy journalists who struggle often blame the changing tides of information consumption, when in reality they’re just struggling to compete for attention. Many have been successful in making the transition, so we don’t think it’s fair to paint all of legacy journalism as having something to learn from news creators. But our message overall would be that traditional news shouldn’t blame consumers for not maintaining their expensive newspaper and cable subscriptions, but instead [should] figure out how to compete and win in this new age.

Srivatchan: For journalists who have been successful in their careers but want to transition to social media, we think they severely underestimate how well-prepared they are to make the jump. They’ve already been writing strong articles and hooks to get people to click. We think journalists underestimate how that skill can translate on a platform like YouTube, where everything is dependent on the packaging that gets someone to click on your video.

Often, when someone from traditional media starts a new Instagram or YouTube page, they make very lo-fi content, talking to their phone with their headphones mic. I think they see influencers doing that and think viewers want authenticity. That works for some people, but our view is that investing in strong production is the baseline expectation on social media.

Instead of seizing the social media opportunity, often, legacy journalism is falling into the trap of liquidating its reputation for more attention and to better monetize its declining assets. It’s partnering with gambling apps — CNN’s partnership with Kalshi, or [Dow Jones’] with Polymarket — and inviting inflammatory internet voices rather than the trusted ones that educate.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Developers can apply to bring apps into AI Mode and the Gemini app, and Google's policy bars misleading descriptions meant to get an app picked.

Google opened a preview of its Connected Apps Platform. Developers can apply for access, and apps Google approves can run inside AI Mode in Search and in the Gemini app.

Google announced the platform on Oct. 28. Robby Stein, VP of Product, Google Search, posted on X Thursday that Google “just opened the public preview.”

When I covered connected apps coming to AI Mode in July, Google hadn’t said how an application gets added to the group of applications that AI Mode could pass work to. Developer documentation has been made available and outlines the path as well as what the policy for the platform is regarding how one app can try to get selected over another.

The developer connects their application to the platform via a remote MCP server (MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, which is the open-standard communication protocol used by AI models in conjunction with external tools) or through AppFunctions, referred to as Android MCP by Google. Google states that using an MCP server provides access to Gemini and Search users on web, Android, and iOS, while the Android MCP route provides access to Gemini users on Android.

The registration process occurs via Google Connected Console. Upon registering the developer will select a category for each of their applications, which establishes the minimum capabilities that the application must have and cannot be altered after registration, according to the Prerequisites Page. In addition to selecting a category for the application, developers will be required to identify a minimum of three capabilities that will be shown to users when determining if they want to connect the application.

The console also asks where each app should be available, by country, language, and Google product. Google reviews and tests each app before it can be published. For apps that need people to sign in, developers must give Google test accounts with sample data, and Google says an app it can’t fully test may be rejected.

Google’s Connected Apps policy says an app can’t reference other tools or create rules for when other tools should be used. In the same list, the policy says connected apps must not:

“deceive or influence the model into performing an adverse action or behavior; for example, using overly broad or deceptive capability descriptions to influence the model into selecting the Connected App over another Connected App.”

Google’s MCP server guide says AI models rely on a server’s instructions “to recognize when to delegate tasks to your server,” and recommends clear instructions so requests route accurately.

This policy excludes ads and promotional materials from other companies within the integration. Apps are allowed to include their own brand information as part of the application. If developers do violate this policy, Google will have the ability to reject the app; suspend access to the app; remove the app from their platform; or suspend/terminate the developer’s account.

On the users’ end, according to Google’s Search help page, when people use AI Mode it may default to the last app they used to complete a task. Users are able to specify a different app to be included with their request. Additionally, they can submit a general search query and then choose from a list of available applications.

There are now connected apps for Search that operate in AI Mode within the United States, specifically in English. The apps listed on the Google help page are Instacart, Canva, YouTube Music, Yahoo Fantasy Football and Sleeper Fantasy Football.

Google has launched over 50 connected apps across Search and Gemini, and states that once a developer puts an app live, they will be able to view traffic, latency and error rates, according to Google’s blog post.

Applicants are able to file an application as well as have their apps reviewed for inclusion in AI Mode using a formal written policy created by Google.

Google’s guide also states that the model goes by your app’s server instructions (e.g., which tasks your app can handle) when deciding whether to pass it a task. Under Google’s policy, an app can’t make overly broad or false claims about what it does in order to trick the model into choosing it over other apps.

As part of its phased roll-out of access to the platform, Google also stated that additional developers, geographic markets, and Google products would be added in the next few months. The coming weeks will see apps from partner companies (including Adobe, Experian, Localiza and Peloton) that are currently available on Gemini become available on Search, as well as a new integration with Calm for both Search and Gemini.

Google Search Advocate John Mueller wrote in a LinkedIn comment that he’s excited about connected apps as a search platform, while calling it “still extremely early.” He noted that he doesn’t work on the product.

Follow on YouTube. Matt G. Southern is the Senior News Writer at Search Engine Journal, where he’s covered Google, SEO, ...

In December, Google launched its News AI pilot program, which licenses content from select publishers and uses it to test new AI features in Google News. On Thursday, the company announced that the program has added new partnerships, bringing the total number of publications in the pilot to more than 400 worldwide.

At launch, the program partnered with international publishers like The Guardian, El País, The Times of India, and The Washington Post. More publications are now coming on board, including CNN, The Financial Times, Axios, and Forbes.

RELATED ARTICLEDiscover isn’t the only place Google is experimenting with AI-generated snippetsAndrew DeckJanuary 26, 2026As part of the expansion, the program has also added local news publishers across the U.S., including The Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina; Oil City News in Casper, Wyoming; the Illinois- and Iowa-based newspaper chain Shaw Media; and the nonprofit newsroom The Texas Tribune.

“People’s information consumption habits are changing, and we want to make sure publishers of all sizes, local newsrooms included, can navigate these shifts,” Brianna Puccini Duff, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement to Nieman Lab.

Google declined to comment on the exact terms of the deals. However, Duff clarified that the News AI pilot does not operate on a “pay-per-value” model, meaning publishers are not compensated based on how much their content contributes to an AI-generated output. (The pay-per-value model is part of a parallel program that pays publishers for content surfaced in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, according to a recent report by Digiday.)

With the News AI pilot, publishers are instead paid to provide content that appears in experimental AI-powered features. That includes “story previews” — in-depth, AI-generated article summaries of recent stories that may show up on a publisher’s Google News page. Here’s a Washington Post example, with a disclaimer noting the copy is AI-generated and “may include mistakes.”

An AI-generated “story preview” on the Google News page for The Washington Post

Another test feature is “audio briefing,” a customizable, AI-generated podcast in the Google News app that stitches together daily headlines. Users can select the topics they’re most interested in hearing about, including “World,” “Gaming,” or “Sports” news. The feature includes citations that link to articles mentioned in the briefing.

#7543. A new report argues newsrooms need to do more experiments — like, the kind with randomization and results

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Mississippi Today had a question. Did the stories around its Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative reporting affect the way those investigations were received?

It’s the kind of question local newsrooms can’t easily test on their own. But researchers from Local NExT Lab at Syracuse University could.

In a national survey, 1,768 adults were shown the same investigation surrounded by a different mix of stories. In one, the investigation was shown alongside positive community stories. (Think: “How a local fossil park changed science history.”) In another, the investigation was featured alongside other investigative stories.

The investigation was rated more accurate, important, and relevant when it was surrounded by community-focused stories, not other investigative stories. (Audience reaction to a third story mix, where the investigation was surrounded by stories about legislation, was not consistent.)

The result was described in the first report from the Local NExT Lab. Joshua Darr, director of the lab and associate professor at Syracuse University, believes that although dashboards and engagement analytics are “very important tools” for newsrooms, they aren’t enough.

“Engagement data can’t tell you what caused audiences to engage, settle a hunch, or isolate your contribution,” the report reads. “Randomization can.”

“The key word there is ’caused,'” Darr added in an email. “Without randomization, you can tell when engagement is up or down or if a particular story is doing well, but it’s hard to know exactly why that is happening.”

RELATED ARTICLESearching for gold: Making sense of academic research about journalismAngie Drobnic HolanApril 27, 2023At Nieman Lab, we often hear from both sides of academic-practitioner partnerships. Researchers wonder why newsrooms don’t pay attention to their findings or fail to respond to their overtures about experiments. Publishers, editors, and journalists, meanwhile, tell me they don’t have time to read dense and jargon-filled academic papers. They can be annoyed by requests to spend time or resources they don’t have. And it’s not always fun to be someone else’s test subject.

When partnering with Local NExT Lab, Darr emphasized, the local newsrooms don’t have to commit money or manpower. They agree to two or three conversations. The researchers listen and then design, field, and analyze the experiments. In return, the newsrooms get their ideas tested and causal evidence.

In another experiment, the Local NExt Lab found that Instagram Reels including reporters’ faces drove the most interest and engagement, but when it came to clicking “follow,” profiles that looked like traditional news brands won out. Respondents chose to follow newsrooms (in this case New Orleans Public Radio) more often than reporter-named accounts.

The first batch of tests was funded by the W.K. Kellogg Foundation. Additional support from the American Journalism Project will allow for further tests on a larger cohort next year. The full report is here.

#7542. Do videos with excessive motion help kids pay attention, or are they just distractions?

A recent study looked into a rising trend in children’s content — and the results suggest that educators should proceed with caution. Researchers at the Indian School of Business and Santa Clara University tracked eye movements on educational videos with moving backgrounds and found that those videos both command attention and deflect it onto the noisy backgrounds.

The study spanned more than 32,000 videos that were tagged as being “made for kids.” The researchers tracked the eye movements of kids between the ages of six and ten and noted the view rates for those clips. Then, background motion was added to those videos, and viewing habits were measured again.

While a wide range of videos were included in the study, the idea of an educational video with unrelated background motion conjures up images of some specific content formats. Perhaps you’ve seen them: They’re videos that pair dense explanations with overlaid footage of oddly satisfying compilations or Minecraft gameplay sessions.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Thanks to so-called “pdf-to-brainrot” generators, those mash-ups have become study aids for some students. They’ve even made it into the realm of politics. In 2024, for example, the Kamala Harris campaign paired World of Warcraft gameplay with a Tim Walz rally.

Clearly, the adults using this split-screen approach believe it keeps eyes glued to the screen, even among viewers with short attention spans. According to the recent study, that idea is only half true. The researchers found that videos with “high motion” had 2% higher view rates compared to more inert content. But those viewers weren’t necessarily keeping their attention on the educational parts of those videos. Instead, the researchers noted that their subjects’ eyes would follow the moving backgrounds rather than the didactic foregrounds.

Distracting as these videos may be, they can serve a beneficial purpose. The researchers suggested that educators should apply the results to harness the attention-grabbing nature of moving backgrounds.

“Motion is a powerful design lever, but it must be used intentionally,” said Madhu Viswanathan, an Associate Professor of Marketing at the Indian School of Business. “Rather than maximizing continuous stimulation throughout a video, creators should use targeted motion to facilitate attention recovery during moments where attention drift is most expected.”

Several apps have already committed to the “TikTokification” of contemporary education. Revyze and ScrollEd are two platforms that try to keep kids focused by presenting them with kinetic learning environments. The popularity of those apps shows that the concept of fast-paced educational videos is catching on with students, but the recent research shows that a methodical approach will be important if students’ scrolling behaviors is to translate to positive learning outcomes.

#7541. Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp.

Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use.

The update, set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab.

The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard. As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request.

RELATED ARTICLE“An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI trainingSarah ScireSeptember 18, 2026“This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.”

In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products.

Here’s the new language about scraping in full:

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.”

Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.”

Meta declined to answer a list of questions about these updated terms. A public affairs spokesperson at the company said in an email that language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads, and this update consolidates them in one place. He also said that the new terms will not change how Meta crawls publishers in the future, and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.”

On its developer page, Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access.

However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content.

RELATED ARTICLEFederal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright winAndrew DeckSeptember 30, 2026Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs).

Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel, a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.”

Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers previously had to consent to their content appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode. As of August 2026, all websites now have the option to opt out.

Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One. The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service.

RELATED ARTICLEMeet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAIAndrew DeckFebruary 20, 2025Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard.

“Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.”

Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook.

Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30.

“I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.”

Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know at [email protected].

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect Google’s current AI search policies.

AI Search Tracking Checklist: How to Attribute Calls From ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity

Research into travel queries suggests that personal experience and subjective judgment may help smaller publishers compete in AI search.

New research from BrightEdge shows that top brands in travel categories dominate the rankings in both ChatGPT and AI Overviews. What’s interesting is that while the BrightEdge data shows that the same brands are dominating travel queries, the top-ranked brands differ according to which sector/niche of travel is being inquired about.

What people choose has generally been biased toward whatever is the most well known. That’s the idea behind advertising, that the more well known a product is, the likelier it is to be chosen by a consumer, and if the consumer is delighted by the choice, they’ll generally stick with that choice (brand loyalty).

So it shouldn’t be surprising that big brands that are well known and trusted by consumers win out for each of their given sectors.

“American Airlines, Royal Caribbean and Expedia lead their categories on both Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT.

Hotels have a different leader on each engine. Hilton leads Google AI Overviews at 28.3%. Marriott leads ChatGPT at 29.4%.

2.2x: Expedia’s visibility compared with Kayak on Google AI Overviews (31.3% vs 14.4%). On ChatGPT, the gap is 1.4x.

38%: share of booking-intent prompts on Google AI Overviews that name a booking platform, against 12% of inspiration prompts.

78%: Booking platforms appear in 78% of budget-related Google AI Overviews answers, compared with 17% of other answers.

9%: Only 9% of tracked Google AI Overviews prompts have booking intent.”

Then elsewhere it shows how brands dominate their categories:

Airlines. American Airlines leads on Google AI Overviews (26.6%) and ChatGPT (25.3%). Its gap to United is 6.1 points on Google AI Overviews and 9.1 points on ChatGPT.

Cruise lines. Royal Caribbean leads on both engines, at 24.8% and 28.8%. Royal Caribbean and Carnival have higher visibility in this ChatGPT sample, while Viking has lower visibility.”

Lastly, the BrightEdge data shows where smaller brands may have an uphill fight competing: Queries with the word “cheap.”

“Booking platforms appear in 78% of tracked Google AI Overviews answers involving terms such as “cheap,” “deal,” “budget” or “last-minute,” compared with 17% of other answers. Expedia appears in 44% of the budget-related answers.

The pattern suggests that price-focused questions are an important area for booking platforms to track. It is an observed association, not evidence that using these words causes a brand to appear.”

One additional thing to point out is that AI search doesn’t link out to sites with rankings in the same way that classic Search does. This is why BrightEdge calls these figures share of voice, rather than rankings of individual search results. They measure appearances among tracked AI answers because AI does not feature traditional ranking positions.

Adding further complexity to understanding the AI results is that the results containing user generated content (UGC) and content with a human experience quality to it tend to rank better for queries that are related to inspiration. There is less domination of big brand rankings for subjective queries, which creates and opening for sites like Reddit and YouTube.

While BrightEdge did not speculate as to the reason why big brands don’t show for those kinds of queries, it may be that queries that require human experience are not the kinds of queries that big brands focus on. That data point may be a bright spot not just for forums and Reddit but also for travel blogs and smaller travel-related sites that can be subjective and can add unique human insights and subjectivity.

BrightEdge says this about what their data shows:

“Platforms and organizations such as YouTube, Reddit and AAA are more prominent in inspiration questions.

Hotels and cruise lines feature more heavily in comparison questions, while booking platforms appear more often in booking-intent questions. Only 9% of tracked Google AI Overviews prompts fall into the booking-intent category.

Inspiration and comparison account for most of this panel, making them important areas for travel brands to measure visibility and competition.”

That means there is an opening for smaller and rising brands to cover areas where human experience, human judgement, and subjective opinion based on experience is valued and sought after by consumers.

Queries that clearly belong in specific categories tend to be dominated by big brands. Like regular search though, the key to breaking into most any niche is to grow awareness of a brand and build trust. Search engine rankings are heavily influenced by user behavior signals and those rankings are then fed up the pipeline to AI chat.

“Categories: hotels, airlines, booking platforms and cruise lines. Non-travel platforms such as YouTube and Reddit are excluded from the category rankings.”

The door into ranking is inspiration and subjectivity, the kinds of things that Reddit tends to rank for. That said, UGC and platform rankings have historically been vulnerable to smart and aggressive content strategies, so I would encourage travel bloggers to eat Reddit’s lunch with expertise because expertise and authoritativeness has never been Reddit’s strength.

Read the full findings at BrightEdge: Holiday Travel in AI Search: The Travel Brands AI Puts on Its List

#7538. Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes

Allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s permissions.

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models.

In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts.

On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service. The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then.

“I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'”

Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.”

Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. The accounts let companies manage Facebook pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place.

As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold):

You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products. Here’s the original text: You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements.
